To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

climate change has limited impacts on wind and solar photovoltaic power generation, but may decrease hydro and thermoelectrical generation by up to 15% and 30% for a 1,5°C and 3°C warming, respectively.
the electricity sector will be vulnerable to the climate change impacts on wind, solar PV, hydropower and conventional thermoelectric power plants in Europe.

the impacts of climate warming on electricity production are relatively limited in the 1.5–2 °C range but may double for a 2–3 °C warming, with impacts on hydropower and thermal electricity generation being more important than on solar and wind power.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electricity sector, which is currently considered mainly from the emission side of climate change.
the vulnerability of power production to climate change and its potential to reduce such vulnerability.
the impacts of climate on electricity production, which is an under-represented area of research in climate change mitigation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the electricity sector is both a major driver of climate change and vulnerable to climate change.
climate change is a threat to the power sector, but the magnitude of the threat is not clear.
, in Europe at least, the impacts on power generation are likely to be small, and the benefits in terms of emissions reductions are large, so that the net effect is beneficial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
climate change impacts on power generation are not negligible, and should be considered in the design of the European energy transition.
climate change is a double-edged sword for electricity production.
climate change will have a negative impact on electricity generation across Europe and that this impact will be more significant with higher global warming.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the context of the Paris Agreement, the electricity sector must be considered on both the emission and the resilience side of the climate equation.
the vulnerability of the electricity sector to climate change should be considered in climate change adaptation strategies.
, in the context of the Paris Agreement, climate impacts on electricity production should not be overlooked.
